screens.title: Deep Dive into Azure SQL Database Performance Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move from broad monitoring to targeted diagnostics that reveal why a database is slow. You will learn how Dynamic Management Views act as real-time windows into server state, how Query Store preserves historical query behavior so you can investigate regressions, and how Azure’s intelligent services provide automated analysis and recommendations. We will also cover how to interpret wait statistics and identify common bottlenecks — C P U, input and output, memory, and blocking — so you can take precise corrective actions. For example, you’ll see how a sudden increase in LCK_M_X waits points to blocking, and how Query Store can reveal if a changed plan coincided with a performance regression. Throughout the chapter you’ll practice safe habits: run diagnostic queries in non-production first, validate automated index recommendations, and avoid forcing plans without testing. By the end you will have a toolbox of queries, interpretations, and processes for diagnosing and improving Azure S Q L performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Performance Monitoring
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Deep Dive into Azure SQL Database Performance Monitoring

Use system DMVs for live diagnostics, Query Store for historical analysis, and Azure intelligent tools to guide tuning. Learn practical queries, safe practices, and how to identify common bottlenecks.

In this lesson

You will inspect DMVs and wait statistics, query Query Store to find top resource consumers, and interpret intelligent recommendations while avoiding common pitfalls.

Why it matters

Precise diagnostics reduce guesswork. Knowing whether an issue is I/O, CPU, memory, or locking leads to targeted fixes and less downtime.

Diagnostic Stack
DMVs (real-time)
Query Store (historical)
Intelligent Insights
Explore Key Topics
DMVs
Live state: sessions, requests, I/O and waits.
Query Store
Historical query text, plans, and runtime statistics.
Intelligent Insights
AI-driven analysis and recommendations, use with caution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical monitoring skills you can apply right away. First, you'll use Dynamic Management Views to diagnose live issues: that means reading session and request DMVs and interpreting input and output and wait counters to find what queries are waiting for. Second, you'll interpret Query Store data to find regressions and top resource consumers; this lets you compare execution plans across time and see when a change caused slower execution. Third, you'll learn to use Intelligent Insights and Performance Recommendations to get AI-assisted root cause suggestions and index guidance, while learning how to validate those suggestions safely. Finally, you'll practice identifying common bottlenecks—C P U, input and output, memory, and blocking—using the right DMVs and metrics so your remediation is targeted. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can verify your skill by running example queries and interpreting results in a non-production test environment.

screens.title: Dynamic Management Views (DMVs)
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic Management Views are built-in server views that reveal current internal state. They are intentionally read-only and designed to expose what the engine is doing now: active sessions, executing requests, input and output counters, lock information, and aggregated wait metrics. You use them during an incident to get a precise snapshot. For example, sys. dm_exec_requests shows currently executing statements with C P U time, logical reads, and blocking session IDs, while sys. dm_exec_sessions shows client and connection metadata. A practical misconception is treating DMVs as a historical log — they are not. DMVs reflect the present moment or accumulated counters since last restart; if a heavy C P U spike has already passed, DMVs alone may not show the offending queries. That’s why pairing DMVs with Query Store is critical. Concrete example: when you see many PAGEIOLATCH waits in sys. dm_os_wait_stats while sys. dm_exec_requests shows long-running reads, you have evidence of input and output-bound work. Key takeaway: DMVs are your live diagnostic lens, fast to run, but use them with context and other tools when investigating past events. Dynamic Management Views (DMVs) means dmvs return current server state and are essential for real-time diagnosis but do not replace historical analysis.. In practical terms, what dmvs are and why they are the first diagnostic stop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DMVs defined
keyIdea.text: DMVs return current server state and are essential for real-time diagnosis but do not replace historical analysis.

content.html:
Core Concept

Dynamic Management Views

Read-only server views that report current engine state. Use them to inspect sessions, requests, waits, and I/O at the moment of analysis.

Examples: sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_exec_sessions
I/O stats: sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats
Waits: sys.dm_os_wait_stats
Key Takeaway

DMVs are your live diagnostic lens: quick to query and essential for operational troubleshooting.

Definition
-- Example: currently running requests with wait types
SELECT
    session_id,
    status,
    command,
    blocking_session_id,
    wait_type,
    wait_time,
    last_wait_type,
    wait_resource,
    cpu_time,
    total_elapsed_time,
    reads,
    writes,
    logical_reads,
    program_name,
    query_text = SUBSTRING(st.text, (r.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
                           ((CASE r.statement_end_offset
                                 WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(st.text)
                                 ELSE r.statement_end_offset
                             END - r.statement_start_offset) / 2) + 1)
FROM
    sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
CROSS APPLY
    sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS st
WHERE
    r.session_id <> @@SPID
ORDER BY
    cpu_time DESC;
Supporting Point
DMVs show current waits and resource usage; use them to capture live contention evidence.
Common Mistake
Expecting DMVs to show historical spikes. They may not if the incident already subsided.

screens.title: Key DMVs to Know
screens.narratorSegment: When you reach for a DMV during an incident, choose the view that answers your diagnostic question. If you want to know who is connected and client metadata, start with sys. dm_exec_sessions. If you need current executing statements, their C P U time, reads, and blocking relationships, run sys. dm_exec_requests and cross apply sys. dm_exec_sql_text to get the S Q L text. For input and output metrics tied to files, use sys. dm_io_virtual_file_stats. To find locks and the blocking chain, inspect sys. dm_tran_locks and join to exec_requests by request session id. A concrete example: if a user reports a slow report, query sys. dm_exec_requests to find active queries against the reporting database, note any blocking_session_id values, and capture the S Q L text for review. A common misconception is running heavy diagnostic queries without considering their cost. Some DMV joins can be expensive on busy systems; test them in a non-production mirror if available. Practice simple, targeted DMV queries first and expand only as needed. The takeaway: know the right DMV for the question you want answered to diagnose quickly and with minimal overhead.

keyIdea.title: Practical DMV targets
keyIdea.text: Choose DMVs based on diagnostic need: sessions, requests, I/O, locks and waits form a focused troubleshooting toolkit.

content.html:
Definition

Key DMVs to Know

Target these DMVs when diagnosing common problems: who is running work, what they run, and where waits occur.

sys.dm_exec_sessions — connection and client details
sys.dm_exec_requests — active requests, CPU, reads, blocking
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats — per-file I/O counters
sys.dm_tran_locks — current locks and resources
Example
-- Inspect blocking and SQL text for active requests SELECT r.session_id, r.blocking_session_id, r.wait_type, r.cpu_time, st.text AS sql_text FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) st WHERE r.session_id <> @@SPID ORDER BY r.cpu_time DESC;
Supporting Point
Cross-apply to get SQL text and use blocking_session_id to trace the blocking chain.
Pro Tip
Avoid wide DMV joins on busy systems; start with the minimal columns you need.
Key Takeaway

Pick the smallest DMV that answers your question to limit diagnostic overhead and speed resolution.

screens.title: Wait Statistics and Their Interpretation
screens.narratorSegment: Wait statistics summarize what resources queries are waiting for and are among the most powerful lenses for root cause analysis. The sys. dm_os_wait_stats view aggregates waits by type; common waits include PAGEIOLATCH or PAGEIOLATCH_EX which point to input and output contention when reads are waiting on physical pages, and LCK_M_X which indicates exclusive lock waits and often signals blocking. When you see a dominant wait category, follow the evidence: high PAGEIOLATCH usually motivates input and output optimization — check indexes, query logical reads, or scale to a higher input and output tier; LCK_M_X motivates looking at blocking chains and transaction patterns. A common misconception is treating every wait as actionable immediately. Waits are symptoms; you must correlate them with active queries and resource metrics. For example, high PAGEIOLATCH with many logical reads on a single expensive query suggests the query needs tuning or an index. Key takeaway: classify the dominant wait, then use DMVs like dm_exec_requests and dm_tran_locks to trace the immediate cause and choose a targeted remediation. Wait Statistics and Their Interpretation means wait types point to the resource class causing delays; correlate waits with queries before acting.. In practical terms, how wait types reveal bottlenecks and where to act. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Waits as evidence
keyIdea.text: Wait types point to the resource class causing delays; correlate waits with queries before acting.

content.html:
Core Concept

Wait Statistics

Use sys.dm_os_wait_stats to see cumulative wait times by type. Interpret the dominant waits to steer your investigation toward CPU, I/O, memory, or locking.

PAGEIOLATCH — I/O/page read waits
LCK_M_X — exclusive lock blocking
CXPACKET — parallelism waits (often CPU-related)
ASYNC_IO_COMPLETION — asynchronous I/O completion
Action pattern: identify the dominant wait, find the queries contributing to it with dm_exec_requests and Query Store, then select targeted remediation such as index tuning, query rewrite, or resource scaling.
Example
-- Summarize waits (sample)
SELECT wait_type, SUM(wait_time_ms) AS total_wait_ms,
       SUM(waiting_tasks_count) AS total_tasks
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT IN ('CLR_SEMAPHORE','LAZYWRITER_SLEEP')
GROUP BY wait_type
ORDER BY total_wait_ms DESC;
Common Mistake
Jumping to scale up before confirming whether slow queries can be tuned. Waits should guide whether tuning or scaling is the right first step.
Key Takeaway

Wait statistics identify the resource class causing delay; use them to choose targeted remediation rather than guessing.

screens.title: Query Store: Historical Query Analytics
screens.narratorSegment: Query Store records query texts, execution plans, and runtime statistics so you can examine historical behavior and detect regressions. Think of Query Store as a flight recorder: it persists plan choices and performance metrics across time windows. This makes it ideal for investigating intermittent or past spikes that DMVs no longer show. You enable Query Store at the database level and then use built-in SSMS reports or query Query Store DMVs such as sys. query_store_query, sys. query_store_plan, and sys. query_store_runtime_stats. A common real-world scenario is a report that suddenly slows after a deployment; Query Store lets you compare plan fingerprints before and after the change and, if appropriate, force the previous plan. A notable misconception is overusing plan forcing without understanding why the plan changed — forced plans can mask underlying issues or harm other queries. Use Query Store to identify the top resource-consuming queries by C P U or logical reads, then validate any forced plan or index before applying it broadly. The takeaway: Query Store shifts troubleshooting from reactive to informed retrospective analysis. Query Store: Historical Query Analytics means query store persists historical query behaviors and plans, enabling regression analysis and targeted plan interventions.. In practical terms, how query store captures plans and runtime statistics to find regressions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Query Store role
keyIdea.text: Query Store persists historical query behaviors and plans, enabling regression analysis and targeted plan interventions.

content.html:
Definition

Query Store

A historical recorder of queries, plans, and runtime stats. Use it to find regressions and compare plans across time.

sys.query_store_query, sys.query_store_plan, sys.query_store_runtime_stats
Built-in reports in SSMS: Top Resource Consuming Queries
Key Takeaway

Use Query Store to attach performance changes to plan changes and to recover a better-known plan when appropriate.

Example Query
-- Top 10 queries by average CPU time from Query Store
SELECT TOP 10
    qt.query_text_id,
    q.query_id,
    qt.query_sql_text,
    SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time) AS total_avg_cpu_time,
    SUM(rs.count_executions) AS total_executions
FROM
    sys.query_store_query_text AS qt
JOIN
    sys.query_store_query AS q
    ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
JOIN
    sys.query_store_plan AS p
    ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN
    sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs
    ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
GROUP BY
    qt.query_text_id, q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
ORDER BY
    total_avg_cpu_time DESC;
Supporting Point
Query Store is persistent; it lets you inspect plan changes after the fact, unlike transient DMV state.

screens.title: Query Store DMVs and Practical Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Query Store exposes DMVs you can query for programmatic analysis or to script reports. The example query here aggregates runtime stats to show the top queries by average C P U time — a straightforward way to find candidates for investigation. When you run this query, note the query text, total executions, and average C P U; then cross-reference the query_id with sys. query_store_plan to inspect different plans and their performance. A common misconception is equating highest C P U with the only problem; also check execution count and logical reads to understand per-execution cost versus cumulative impact. Concrete walkthrough: run the provided top 10 by C P U query, pick the top row, get its query_id, and then query sys. query_store_plan for that query_id to list available plans and their plan_id. Next, query sys. query_store_runtime_stats for those plan_ids to see runtime differences. If a newer plan shows worse performance, consider forcing the prior plan after testing. Remember to keep Query Store retention settings and size limits in mind; in very busy systems, configure appropriate capture policies. Closing question: after you find a top C P U query, what additional metric will you check to decide between indexing, rewriting, or scaling?

keyIdea.title: Query Store workflow
keyIdea.text: Use Query Store DMVs to identify resource-heavy queries, compare plans, and decide on corrective actions after validation.

content.html:
Process

Query Store Code Walkthrough

Run these DMVs to surface top CPU consumers, then inspect plans and runtime stats for regression analysis.

-- Top 10 queries by average CPU time from Query Store SELECT TOP 10 qt.query_text_id, q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text, SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time) AS total_avg_cpu_time, SUM(rs.count_executions) AS total_executions FROM sys.query_store_query_text AS qt JOIN sys.query_store_query AS q ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id JOIN sys.query_store_plan AS p ON q.query_id = p.query_id JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id GROUP BY qt.query_text_id, q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text ORDER BY total_avg_cpu_time DESC;
Next Steps
1. Select top query_id from result. 2. Query sys.query_store_plan for that query_id and list plan_id and plan hash. 3. Query sys.query_store_runtime_stats filtered by plan_id to compare performance.
Pro Tip
Also check execution count: a moderate-cost query with millions of executions may have higher cumulative cost than a single expensive one.
Key Takeaway

Combine average per-execution metrics with execution counts and plan comparisons to prioritize actions.

screens.title: Using SSMS Query Store Reports — Hands-on Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When using SSMS Query Store reports you follow a clear workflow: enable Query Store if needed, generate workload to populate data, open the 'Top Resource Consuming Queries' report, select a metric and time window, and then drill into a specific query to view plan and runtime history. Begin by choosing a metric such as total C P U time or logical reads, and set the time interval to the period that experienced the problem. Then click a query in the top pane and examine the bottom pane for plan comparisons and runtime trends. Process Flow
  1. Enable Query Store in the target database and configure retention and capture settings.
  2. Generate workload to ensure Query Store captures relevant activity for the time window you will analyze.

Check

Relying solely on the highest CPU metric without checking execution counts and plan differences can mis-prioritize work.

screens.title: Intelligent Insights and Performance Recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Intelligent Insights applies automated analysis to database telemetry and can highlight anomalies, possible root causes, and remediation suggestions. Performance Recommendations can suggest or even automatically apply index changes and parameterization strategies. These features speed discovery, but the most important operational rule is to validate before you accept. For example, an automated index recommendation might improve one heavy reporting query but inadvertently slow down a transactional path. A good practice is to test recommendations in a staging environment and measure query-level before-and-after metrics. Another misconception is treating automated recommendations as authoritative; they are suggestions based on heuristics and observed workload patterns. The correct sequence is: review the recommendation, understand which queries and plans it affects, test its impact on representative workload, and then schedule controlled deployment. In short, use Intelligent Insights to surface likely problems and Performance Recommendations to accelerate tuning, but keep human validation as the final gatekeeper. Comparison

Intelligent Insights vs Performance Recommendations

Intelligent Insights: anomaly detection, root cause hints, and narrative explanations.
Performance Recommendations: index suggestions, parameterization help, and optional automatic tuning actions.
Guideline
Treat insights as diagnostic leads and recommendations as candidate changes. Validate both with representative tests before applying.
Concrete Scenario
Intelligent Insights flags a sudden degradation for a reporting workload and recommends a non-clustered index. Test by creating the index in staging, replay representative queries, and compare CPU and logical reads before applying to production.

Automated tools accelerate discovery but require human validation to ensure changes benefit overall workload.

screens.title: Common Performance Bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Performance problems usually boil down to a few resource classes. C P U bottlenecks appear when the engine spends excessive time processing queries, often caused by inefficient queries, missing indexes, or excessive parallelism. input and output bottlenecks appear as PAGEIOLATCH waits and long disk queues; the remedy may be query tuning to reduce logical reads, better indexing, or moving to a higher input and output service tier. Memory bottlenecks show as insufficient cache hit ratios and increased paging; they can be improved by increasing cache size or reducing memory pressure via query tuning. Blocking is a logical phenomenon where one transaction holds locks needed by others; look for blocking_session_id in sys. dm_exec_requests and inspect dm_tran_locks to find the chain. A common misconception is upgrading compute immediately; sometimes targeted tuning reduces load enough to avoid additional cost. The practical approach is to identify the dominant resource via waits and counters, find the offending query or pattern with DMVs and Query Store, and then choose the least disruptive, verifiable fix. Core Concept

Common Bottlenecks

CPU: inefficient plans, missing indexes, expensive scalar functions. Check CPU time in dm_exec_requests and Query Store.
I/O: PAGEIOLATCH waits and high logical reads. Check io virtual file stats and query logical reads.
Memory: low cache hit ratios and paging; examine buffer usage and plan cache pressure.
Blocking: LCK_M_X waits and blocking_session_id chains in dm_exec_requests and dm_tran_locks.
Scenario
If you see high CPU and many CXPACKET waits, investigate parallelism, check expensive missing-index candidates, and review plan operators for excessive work per row.
Remediation Checklist
  • Identify top queries by resource from Query Store.
  • Inspect execution plans for scans, sorts, or nested loops on large rowsets.
  • Test index or query changes in staging and measure before/after metrics.
Key Takeaway

Correct diagnosis determines whether to tune queries, change indexes, or scale resources; don’t assume scaling is the first step.

Analyze Query Store Data

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move from broad monitoring to targeted diagnostics that reveal why a database is slow. You will learn how Dynamic Management Views act as real-time windows into server state, how Query Store preserves historical query behavior so you can investigate regressions, and how Azure’s intelligent services provide automated analysis and recommendations. We will also cover how to interpret wait statistics and identify common bottlenecks — C P U, input and output, memory, and blocking — so you can take precise corrective actions. For example, you’ll see how a sudden increase in LCK_M_X waits points to blocking, and how Query Store can reveal if a changed plan coincided with a performance regression. Throughout the chapter you’ll practice safe habits: run diagnostic queries in non-production first, validate automated index recommendations, and avoid forcing plans without testing. By the end you will have a toolbox of queries, interpretations, and processes for diagnosing and improving Azure S Q L performance.

These objectives focus on practical monitoring skills you can apply right away. First, you'll use Dynamic Management Views to diagnose live issues: that means reading session and request DMVs and interpreting input and output and wait counters to find what queries are waiting for. Second, you'll interpret Query Store data to find regressions and top resource consumers; this lets you compare execution plans across time and see when a change caused slower execution. Third, you'll learn to use Intelligent Insights and Performance Recommendations to get AI-assisted root cause suggestions and index guidance, while learning how to validate those suggestions safely. Finally, you'll practice identifying common bottlenecks—C P U, input and output, memory, and blocking—using the right DMVs and metrics so your remediation is targeted. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can verify your skill by running example queries and interpreting results in a non-production test environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied tasks you will practice. First, you will run the provided diagnostic queries to retrieve top C P U-consuming queries from Query Store and compare those results with SSMS reports. This helps you match textual query IDs and execution plans with observed resource spikes. Second, you will query sys. dm_exec_requests and cross-apply sql text to inspect currently running requests, their wait types, and blocking_session_id to understand live contention. Third, you will practice reading sys. dm_os_wait_stats to classify waits such as PAGEIOLATCH or LCK_M_X and tie them to an action like reindexing or investigating blocking chains. Fourth, you will exercise safe tuning: enable Query Store in a test database, simulate workload, view top resource consumers, and validate any recommendations before applying them. Each task has a milestone you can confirm in a non-production environment, so you leave this chapter with repeatable diagnostic steps.

Dynamic Management Views are built-in server views that reveal current internal state. They are intentionally read-only and designed to expose what the engine is doing now: active sessions, executing requests, input and output counters, lock information, and aggregated wait metrics. You use them during an incident to get a precise snapshot. For example, sys. dm_exec_requests shows currently executing statements with C P U time, logical reads, and blocking session IDs, while sys. dm_exec_sessions shows client and connection metadata. A practical misconception is treating DMVs as a historical log — they are not. DMVs reflect the present moment or accumulated counters since last restart; if a heavy C P U spike has already passed, DMVs alone may not show the offending queries. That’s why pairing DMVs with Query Store is critical. Concrete example: when you see many PAGEIOLATCH waits in sys. dm_os_wait_stats while sys. dm_exec_requests shows long-running reads, you have evidence of input and output-bound work. Key takeaway: DMVs are your live diagnostic lens, fast to run, but use them with context and other tools when investigating past events. When you reach for a DMV during an incident, choose the view that answers your diagnostic question. If you want to know who is connected and client metadata, start with sys. dm_exec_sessions. If you need current executing statements, their C P U time, reads, and blocking relationships, run sys. dm_exec_requests and cross apply sys. dm_exec_sql_text to get the S Q L text. For input and output metrics tied to files, use sys. dm_io_virtual_file_stats. To find locks and the blocking chain, inspect sys. dm_tran_locks and join to exec_requests by request session id. A concrete example: if a user reports a slow report, query sys. dm_exec_requests to find active queries against the reporting database, note any blocking_session_id values, and capture the S Q L text for review. A common misconception is running heavy diagnostic queries without considering their cost. Some DMV joins can be expensive on busy systems; test them in a non-production mirror if available. Practice simple, targeted DMV queries first and expand only as needed. The takeaway: know the right DMV for the question you want answered to diagnose quickly and with minimal overhead.

Wait statistics summarize what resources queries are waiting for and are among the most powerful lenses for root cause analysis. The sys. dm_os_wait_stats view aggregates waits by type; common waits include PAGEIOLATCH or PAGEIOLATCH_EX which point to input and output contention when reads are waiting on physical pages, and LCK_M_X which indicates exclusive lock waits and often signals blocking. For example, high PAGEIOLATCH with many logical reads on a single expensive query suggests the query needs tuning or an index.
